draft.title: Brain ablation and lesioning
card: the removal of part of the brain. Researchers then watch how the animal's behaviour changes.
the damage of part of the brain, for example by cutting it or destroying its cells, without taking it out. Again, the change in behaviour is observed.
If a function is lost or changed after a part is removed or damaged, that part is likely to play a role in that function. This links brain areas to jobs.
These methods were used on animals, not people, because they cause permanent harm. Results from animals may not match the human brain exactly.
draft.remember: Take out or damage a brain area, then watch what changes, to link that area to a function.

a.q: What do researchers do in a brain lesioning study?
opts: Damage part of an animal's brain and observe behaviour
Scan an animal's brain while it completes a task
Measure the bumps on an animal's skull
Ask an animal's owner about its behaviour
a.why: Lesioning means damaging a brain area and watching what changes in behaviour. Scanning an active brain is neuroimaging, which does not damage the brain, so it is not lesioning.
a.clue: Think about what is done to the brain itself.

b.q: Researchers remove a small brain area from rats. The rats can still move normally but no longer find their way through a maze they had learned. What can the researchers reasonably conclude?
opts: The removed area is likely involved in finding the way
The removed area controls all movement in rats
The removed area has no function in rats
The same area must do this job in human brains
b.why: A loss of a function after removal suggests that the area plays a role in it. Movement stayed normal, so the area is not shown to control movement. Animal results may not match humans exactly, so the human claim goes too far.
b.clue: Which function was lost, and which stayed the same?

a.best: Damage part of an animal's brain and observe behaviour

b.best: The removed area is likely involved in finding the way

problems.detail: "These methods were used on animals, not people" is too absolute. Ablation and lesioning have been done on humans for treatment, for example lobotomy, split-brain surgery (corpus callosotomy) and hemispherectomy, and this is commonly taught in VCE. Say "mainly on animals" or "in research, mostly on animals" instead.

The right option is the only one with a hedge ("likely"). The wrong options all use absolutes ("all", "must", "no function"), so a student could pick the answer from test-taking strategy alone without understanding the idea.
